sections.readable_text: Chloe is reading a novel and wants to finish at least [MATH: 18\,000] words this evening. She reads at a pace of [MATH: 300] words per minute. What is the fewest number of minutes she must read to meet her goal?

sections.normalized_html:
This is a rate problem involving reading speed and time. We use the relationship

[MATH: \text{words} = \text{rate} \times \text{time}.]

Let [MATH: t] be the number of minutes Chloe reads. Since she reads at a pace of [MATH: 300] words per minute, the total number of words read is

[MATH: 300t.]

She wants to read at least [MATH: 18\,000] words, so we write this as the following inequality:

[MATH: 300t \geq 18\,000]

Now, we divide both sides by [MATH: 3\,000] to obtain

[MATH: t \geq 60.]

So, Chloe must read for at least [MATH: 60] minutes. Since the question asks for the fewest number of minutes, the answer is [MATH: 60.]

sections.normalized_html:
We are given a scenario with a fixed cost and a per-participant cost. We are told the total cost must not exceed [MATH: \[math]200,] and we are asked to find the maximum number of participants the tutor can afford.

Let [MATH: x] be the number of participants.

The total cost is the fixed fee plus the per-participant fee:

[MATH: \text{Total cost} = 35 + 18.25x]

We are told this total must not exceed [MATH: \[/math]200,] so we write the inequality:

[MATH: 35 + 18.25x \leq 200]

We now solve the inequality for [MATH: x{:}]

[MATH: 35 + 18.25x|≤ 200; 18.25x|≤ 200 − 35; 18.25x|≤ 165; x|≤ (165)/(18.25); x|≤ 9.0410…]

Since [MATH: x] must be a whole number, the greatest possible number of participants is [MATH: 9.]
